sections.h2: What the Maryland homestead credit does
sections.html:
In Maryland, "homestead" usually means the Homestead Property Tax Credit. It limits how fast the taxable assessment on your principal residence can climb. It does not knock a fixed dollar amount off the value of your home.

Every county and municipality must hold annual increases in taxable assessment to 10% or less. The credit appears on a bill only in years when the phased-in assessment grows faster than the cap. In a flat year you may see no credit at all, and that does not mean your application was lost.

For a seller the credit matters in two ways. It has been lowering the bill you carry now, and it does not travel with the house. A buyer has to qualify on their own after the deed is recorded.

The credit is the portion of the assessment increase above the cap, multiplied by the tax rate. Under Tax-Property § 9-105(e), State and bicounty taxes use a fixed 110% of the prior year's taxable assessment, while each county or municipality picks a percentage between 100% and 110% for its own tax.

Think of it in steps. Start with last year's taxable assessment, then find the new phased-in assessment. Apply the cap to get the highest assessment the bill may use. Whatever sits above that limit is shielded, and the credit equals the tax on that shielded amount at the applicable rate.

Credits under $1 are not granted. Each county sets its own local cap, so check the county's current tax rate sheet for the percentage that applies to your address.

You qualify if the house is your principal residence, you hold a legal interest in it, and nothing in the prior year disqualified the property. The conditions:

  • You live in the home at least six months of the year, including July 1 of the credit year. Illness or a need for special care can excuse an absence.
  • You claim the credit on one property only.
  • The property was not transferred to new ownership in the prior tax year.
  • The owner did not request a zoning change that raised the value, and the use of the property did not change substantially.
  • The prior assessment was not clearly erroneous.

Section 9-105 defines a homeowner broadly. Sole ownership, joint ownership, tenancy by the entireties, a cooperative membership, a land installment contract and a life estate can all count as a legal interest.

There are carve-outs. If an accident or natural disaster damages the home, eligibility can continue for the current year and two more. An owner who razes the house or makes substantial improvements keeps eligibility by having lived there as a principal residence for at least three full tax years before the work, and by finishing within the next tax year. Federal employees stationed outside Maryland can keep it for up to six consecutive years.

sections.h2: How to apply and check your status
sections.html:
You file one application, and it carries forward as long as you keep qualifying. A 2007 law (Tax-Property § 9-105) created the one-time requirement, and the Maryland One Stop portal has taken applications since September 11, 2023.

  • Apply online at Maryland One Stop or through the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) homestead site.
  • Download the paper form in English or Spanish and mail it to the Homestead Tax Credit Division, 700 East Pratt Street, 2nd Floor, Suite 2700, Baltimore, MD 21202, or fax it to 410-225-9344.
  • Do not email an application that contains a Social Security number or a tax return.
  • Look up your property in SDAT's Real Property search. A status of Approved or Application Received needs no action, while No Application means you should file.

The SDAT questions line is 410-767-2165 in the Baltimore area and 1-866-650-8783 elsewhere in Maryland. A final denial can be appealed within 30 days to the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board for the property's jurisdiction. The statute refers to May 1 as a date for the application, so file as early as you can.

sections.h2: When you sell a Maryland house
sections.html:
The credit ends for you at the sale, since a transfer for consideration disqualifies the property for the following year. The new owner must file their own application.

The state works to make that hand-off hard to miss. Since 2021 (Chapter 333), a residential sales contract must carry a statement that a buyer who plans to live in the home may qualify for the homestead property tax credit, plus the SDAT web address. Under § 9-105(f), the settlement agent must give the buyer the application document at settlement, and SDAT mails an application to new owners once the deed is recorded and its records update.

One timing rule helps in a few sales. If a deed is dated in one year but recorded between July 1 and September 1 of the next, the buyer can ask SDAT to treat the deed date as the transfer date. The request is due by September 1 of the second year after the deed date and must include a copy of the executed deed.

Inherited houses follow different rules, covered next.

sections.h2: Heirs and the income-based Homeowners' Tax Credit
sections.html:
Heirs not yet on the record title may qualify for the Homeowners' Tax Credit for up to three taxable years while the title transfer is finalized. They need the will, trust or other instrument, a death certificate, proof of relationship, and the names and addresses of all heirs.

This is a separate program with its own tests. Combined gross household income cannot exceed $60,000, and net worth, not counting the home or qualified retirement savings, must be under $200,000. Only tax on the first $300,000 of assessed value counts, and water and sewer charges are not covered.

The credit is the amount by which your property tax exceeds that limit. Call SDAT to confirm the current figures. Apply by April 15 to see the credit on the July bill. The filing deadline is October 1 each year. Buyers should apply at least 30 days before settlement to receive the credit at the closing table.

The exemptions in Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 11-504 are small, and the one for an owner-occupied home applies only in bankruptcy. A debtor can elect up to $6,000 in cash or property within 30 days of attachment or levy, and up to $500 in a bank account is exempt without electing, with the two combined capped at $6,000.

In a bankruptcy case, § 11-504 also covers owner-occupied residential property, including a condominium or cooperative unit used as a home, up to the federal amount in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(1) adjusted for inflation. Spouses cannot both claim it in the same case, and an eight-year lookback applies to earlier successful claims on the same property.

This is a different idea from the tax credit, and the two are easy to confuse. A seller facing judgments, liens or a pending bankruptcy should talk with a Maryland attorney before signing a contract.

sections.h2: Penalties for claiming the credit wrongly
sections.html:
Someone who does not qualify must pay all the property tax otherwise due for each year of ineligibility. Willful misrepresentation adds a penalty of 25% of the credit received for each affected year, and that penalty becomes a lien on the property.

That lien is why a seller should confirm the status of a former second home or a rented-out house before listing. Owners should report a property that has stopped being a principal residence to the local assessment office by email or phone. A lien of that kind is a title issue and must be cleared before closing.

sections.h2: Selling for cash with the credit in play
sections.html:
A cash sale leaves the tax rules alone but shortens the time you have to tidy things up. Before accepting an offer, gather your latest tax bill, the SDAT property record showing your homestead status, and any notice about a prior-year credit.

  • Ask SDAT or your local assessment office whether the status shows Approved.
  • Check whether any tax is unpaid or any credit has been reversed.
  • If you are an heir, confirm whether you are on the record title yet.

Because the credit does not transfer, your buyer's first bill after closing can look different from yours. That is normal and reflects the buyer's own application, not an error in the sale.

faqs.q: Does Maryland have a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Maryland has a Homestead Property Tax Credit and no flat exemption. It limits yearly increases in the taxable assessment on your principal residence to 10% or less, and local governments may set a lower cap.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply every year?
faqs.a: No. The homestead application is a one-time filing. The separate Homeowners' Tax Credit is applied for each year, with an October 1 deadline.

faqs.q: Does the credit transfer to the buyer when I sell?
faqs.a: No. A sale for consideration disqualifies the property for the following year, so the buyer must file a new application. The settlement agent is required to hand the buyer the application at closing.

faqs.q: How do I know if I already have the credit?
faqs.a: Search the property in SDAT's Real Property database. Approved or Application Received means no action is needed, and No Application means you should file.

faqs.q: Can I keep the credit on a house I inherited?
faqs.a: Possibly for a limited time. Heirs not yet on the record title may qualify for the Homeowners' Tax Credit for up to three taxable years while title is finalized, with documents such as the will and death certificate.
